subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a transverse wave, how do the vibrations relate to the direction in which the wave transfers energy?
options: Perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer
Parallel to the direction of energy transfer
In the same direction as the energy transfer
In a circular path around the energy transfer
questions.explain: In a transverse wave the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.

questions.q: Sound travelling through air is an example of which type of wave?
questions.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave in which air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a longitudinal wave?
options: Vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, producing compressions and rarefactions
Vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, producing crests and troughs
The wave can only travel through a vacuum
The wave carries no energy from one place to another
questions.explain: Longitudinal waves oscillate along the direction of travel, creating regions of compression and rarefaction.

questions.q: In a longitudinal wave, the regions where the particles are pushed close together are called:
questions.explain: Compressions are the regions where particles are bunched together; rarefactions are where they are spread apart.

questions.q: Which of the following is a transverse wave?
options: Ripples on the surface of water
A pressure wave along a stretched slinky pushed end-to-end
questions.explain: Water surface ripples are transverse, with the water oscillating up and down as the wave moves horizontally.

questions.q: The amplitude of a wave is defined as:
options: The maximum displacement of a point from its rest (equilibrium) position
The distance between two adjacent crests
The number of waves passing a point each second
The speed at which the wave travels
questions.explain: Amplitude is the greatest displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position.

questions.q: The wavelength of a wave is best described as:
options: The distance between a point on one wave and the equivalent point on the next wave
The height of a crest above the rest position
The time taken for one complete wave to pass
The number of complete waves produced each second
questions.explain: Wavelength is the distance between two adjacent identical points, such as crest to crest.

questions.q: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.explain: Frequency is measured in hertz, where one hertz is one wave per second.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 1 Hz. This means that:
options: One complete wave passes a point each second
The wave travels 1 metre each second
The wave lasts for one second in total
questions.explain: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, so 1 Hz means one wave per second.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates wave speed (v), frequency (f) and wavelength (λ)?
questions.explain: The wave equation states wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
questions.explain: Using v = f × λ = 50 × 2 = 100 m/s.

questions.q: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
questions.explain: Rearranging v = f × λ gives λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 170 = 2 m.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 200 Hz. What is its time period?
questions.explain: The period T = 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ 200 = 0.005 s.

questions.q: How are the time period (T) and frequency (f) of a wave related?
questions.explain: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, so T = 1/f.

questions.q: If the frequency of a wave increases while its speed stays constant, its wavelength will:
questions.explain: Since v = f × λ at constant speed, increasing frequency means wavelength must decrease.

questions.q: The law of reflection states that:
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of reflection
The reflected ray travels along the normal
The angle of reflection depends on the wave's colour
questions.explain: For reflection, the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection.

questions.q: When measuring the angle of incidence and angle of reflection, the angles are measured from which line?
options: The normal (a line at 90° to the surface)
The direction of the incoming light
questions.explain: Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured between the ray and the normal to the surface.

questions.q: Refraction of a wave occurs because, when it passes from one medium into another, there is a change in its:
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed as it enters a different medium, which can change its direction.

questions.q: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block. Which best describes what happens?
options: It slows down and bends towards the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
It speeds up and bends away from the normal
questions.explain: Light slows when entering the denser glass, so it refracts towards the normal.

questions.q: When light is reflected from a rough surface so that it scatters in many directions, this is called:
questions.explain: A rough surface scatters reflected rays in many directions, producing diffuse reflection.
